key_insight: AI translations of literary texts can be good enough on content and basic fluency, but readers still prefer human translations for immersion and literary feel. In other words, “fine” machine translation is not the same as a satisfying reading experience.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the gap between standard machine translation evaluation and how real readers experience literary translations. It asks whether LLM-based translation can match human translation not just in adequacy, but in immersion and aesthetic impact.
method: Asked 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations with machine translations produced by an agentic LLM-based pipeline.
Focused on reader experience rather than only automatic metrics, looking at immersion, literary effect, and overall preference.
Evaluated translation quality in the context of literary reading, where fluency and adequacy scores alone may miss important differences.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that improving translation quality requires more than optimizing benchmark scores. If the goal is literary translation, evaluation should include human-centered measures like enjoyment, style, and emotional resonance.
